title: What someone said
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -dago REPORTS, AND WHAT IT ATTACHES TO IS THE PLAIN STYLE. gayo becomes gandago and masisseoyo becomes masitdago, so the plain form finally appears on the page here — BOUND inside a report, never as a sentence anybody says. L3 does not lift the ban this course opened with: banmal is still never written free-standing, jeo is still never na, and informal is still never chipped anywhere.

AN ACTION VERB INSERTS AN n, A DESCRIBING VERB DOES NOT. ondago, gandago and baeundago against masitdago, jotago and eopdago. That is the one shape rule of the module, and it splits the verbs the same way M2's -neun and -(eu)n already did.

KOREAN DOES NOT BACKSHIFT. What the person said stays in the tense they said it in: Chingu-ga naeil ondago haesseoyo is 'my friend said he is coming tomorrow', with the present exactly as spoken. English moves the tense back one step and Korean never does, so there is nothing here to learn except to stop doing it.

WHAT DOES CHANGE IS THE PERSON. The jeo inside the quote becomes whoever you are reporting, and then it simply disappears, because M1's law says a subject the listener already knows is not named again. Leaving jeo in reports your own words instead of theirs.

FIVE SHAPES, SORTED BY WHAT WAS SAID RATHER THAN BY WHO SAID IT. A statement takes -dago, a noun with the copula takes -(i)rago, a command takes -(eu)rago, a suggestion takes -jago and a question takes -nyago. All five then hand off to one ordinary verb: L1-M5's haesseoyo for said, and mureosseoyo for asked.

A REPORTED COMMAND LOSES ITS POLITENESS ENDING. The teacher said oseyo, and the report is orago; L2-M1's -(eu)seyo cannot survive inside one. The respect is carried by the title and by the register chip instead. A reported suggestion is -jago, which is also where M4's missing 'let us' finally has somewhere to go.

HONORIFICS INSIDE A REPORT USE ONLY WHAT THE COURSE ALREADY OWNS. malsseum is the word for a raised person's speech, against mal for everybody else's. The productive past honorific -(eu)syeosseoyo and the honorific subject particle -kkeseo are L3-M8's and are not borrowed early. Reports of an elder's words chip formal and everything else stays neutral.

sentences.cue: My friend said he's coming tomorrow.

words.note: L2-M3's wayo in its plain shape onda, plus -dago. The plain style is only ever seen bound inside a report like this; it is never a sentence you say.

sentences.trap: KOREAN DOES NOT BACKSHIFT. English turns 'I'm coming tomorrow' into 'he was coming tomorrow'; Korean keeps the present the friend actually used. Moving the tense back is the single commonest English habit in this module.

variations.cue: My friend said he's coming today.
variations.changed: the day inside the quote

variations.cue: Minsu said he's coming tomorrow.
variations.changed: a named speaker, with M1's -neun on somebody already in the account

mistake.why: That is the English backshift. He said he is coming, so the report keeps the present: Chingu-ga naeil ondago haesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Passing on what somebody told you about their plans.
sentences.mnemonic: The tense stays as it was said.

sentences.cue: My friend said this restaurant is good.

words.note: L2-M5's masisseoyo in its plain shape masitda, plus -go. A describing verb takes the bare -da, with no n inserted the way ondago has one.
L1-M9's joayo reported. The stem ends in h, which turns the following d aspirate, so it is said and written jotago — the same change as M3's jochi.

sentences.trap: -dago ATTACHES TO THE PLAIN STEM, NOT TO THE -yo FORM. There is no masisseoyo-dago. Every report in this module is built by stripping the -yo sentence back to its plain shape first, and that is the whole of the work.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga i-SIK-dang-i ma-SIT-da-go HAE-sseo-yo. masitdago is said ma-sit-tta-go.

variations.cue: My friend said the bibimbap is good.
variations.changed: the dish rather than the restaurant

variations.cue: My friend said this restaurant is good.
variations.changed: jotago, a second describing verb on the same frame

mistake.why: -dago goes on the plain stem, never on the finished -yo verb: Chingu-ga i-sikdang-i masitdago haesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Recommending somewhere on somebody else's word.
sentences.mnemonic: Strip to the plain stem first.

sentences.cue: My friend said she's learning Korean.

words.note: L1-M3's baewoyo reported. It is an action verb, so the plain shape inserts an n before the -da: baeunda, then baeundago.

sentences.trap: THE I INSIDE THE QUOTE DISAPPEARS. She said jeo-neun hangungmal-eul baewoyo. Reported, the jeo is not replaced by another pronoun — it is simply dropped, because chingu-ga at the head has already said whose learning it is.

variations.cue: My younger sibling said they're learning Korean.
variations.changed: L2-M2's dongsaeng as the speaker

variations.cue: My friend said she's learning at the university.
variations.changed: M2's daehak-eseo inside the quote instead of the object

mistake.why: The jeo inside the quote is your friend, not you, so it drops: Chingu-ga hangungmal-eul baeundago haesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody what a friend is up to.
sentences.mnemonic: The person changes; the tense does not.

words.note: L1-M1's haksaeng-ieyo reported. The copula takes -irago after a consonant, and the hyphen sits where it always does in this course: at the copula boundary.
The same ending after a vowel, where the i drops: uisa-rago, not uisa-irago. It is the copula's own allomorph pair, exactly as -ieyo and -yeyo already were.

sentences.trap: A NOUN REPORT IS NOT A -dago REPORT. What is being reported here is a copula sentence, so the ending is -(i)rago. English uses the same 'that' for both, which is why the choice has to be made on the Korean side.
sentences.sound: MIN-su-neun hak-saeng-I-ra-go HAE-sseo-yo. haksaeng-irago is said hak-saeng-i-ra-go.

variations.cue: Yuna said she's a doctor.
variations.changed: a vowel-final noun, so the ending loses its i

variations.cue: Minsu said that I'm a student.
variations.changed: a clause subject inside the report, which takes M2's je-ga

mistake.why: A noun report takes the copula's own ending: Minsu-neun haksaeng-irago haesseoyo.

sentences.cue: The teacher said to come tomorrow.

words.cue: that (you) should come — a reported order
words.note: L2-M4's oseyo reported. The command loses its -(eu)seyo entirely: orago is what the report keeps, and the respect moves onto the title instead.

words.cue: that (you) should wait — a reported order
words.note: L2-M8's gidaryeoyo in the same shape. A stem ending in a vowel takes plain -rago, so gidarirago and orago are built identically.

sentences.trap: THE POLITENESS DOES NOT SURVIVE THE REPORT. She said oseyo and you say orago. That is not rudeness: an ending like -(eu)seyo belongs to the sentence somebody actually spoke, and a report is your sentence, not theirs.

variations.cue: The teacher said to wait a moment.
variations.changed: a different order, with L2-M1's jom inside the quote

variations.cue: My friend said to come tomorrow.
variations.changed: a friend rather than a teacher — the same words, a neutral line

mistake.why: A reported order takes the bare command form: Seonsaengnim-i naeil orago haesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Passing on an instruction from somebody senior.

sentences.cue: My friend said let's go together.

words.cue: that (we) should go — a reported suggestion
words.note: The reported shape of a suggestion. This is where 'let us' finally lands in this course: free-standing it would need -(eu)psida, which is L4-M7's, but reported it is simply -jago.

words.cue: that (we) should eat — a reported suggestion
words.note: L1-M3's meogeoyo in the same shape. The ending is -jago on any stem, with nothing added for a consonant: meokjago, gajago.

sentences.trap: REPORTING A SUGGESTION IS EASIER THAN MAKING ONE. M4 could not write 'let us' at all, because the ending for it belongs to a speech level this course does not teach. Inside a report there is no such problem: -jago is the whole of it.

variations.cue: My friend said let's eat together.
variations.changed: eating rather than going

variations.cue: My younger sibling said let's go together.
variations.changed: a different speaker

mistake.why: The report takes the plain suggestion form on its own: Chingu-ga gachi gajago haesseoyo.

sentences.cue: My friend asked whether I'm coming tomorrow.

words.note: A reported question. There is no separate word for 'whether' or 'if' anywhere in it: the ending -nyago carries the whole of that job.
The same ending on L1-M4's gayo. It goes straight onto the stem, so ganyago and onyago are built the same way.
The second and last verb the module needs. A reported question hands off to mureosseoyo, while everything else in this module hands off to haesseoyo.

sentences.trap: THERE IS NO WORD FOR 'WHETHER'. English needs one to report a yes-or-no question and Korean puts the whole of it in the ending. A learner who goes looking for the missing word will not find one, because -nyago already said it.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga NAE-il O-nya-go mu-REO-sseo-yo. mureosseoyo is said mu-reo-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: My friend asked where I'm going.
variations.changed: L1-M7's eodi-e, so it becomes a where-question

variations.cue: My friend asked whether I'm coming today.
variations.changed: the day inside the question

mistake.why: A reported question takes -nyago on the plain stem, never the finished -yo verb: Chingu-ga naeil onyago mureosseoyo.

sentences.usage: Relaying a question somebody put to you.

words.note: Korean judges the WORDS rather than the person: chingu mal-i majayo, my friend's words are correct. Saying chingu-ga majayo would grade the friend instead.

sentences.trap: KOREAN AGREES WITH THE WORDS, NOT THE PERSON. English says 'my friend is right' and Korean makes the speech the subject of M3's majayo. There is no possessive particle in between either: chingu mal-i, two nouns simply stood next to each other.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu MA-ri MA-ja-yo. mal-i is said ma-ri.

variations.cue: My friend is always right.
variations.changed: M1's hangsang, and the topic particle because the words are already in the account

variations.cue: My friend is wrong.
variations.changed: M3's teullyeoyo, the other half of the pair

mistake.why: majayo grades what was said: Chingu mal-i majayo. With chingu-ga it would be claiming the friend is the correct one.

sentences.usage: Backing somebody up in an argument you were not part of.
sentences.mnemonic: The words are right, not the person.

sentences.cue: What the teacher says is always right.

words.note: The honorific twin of mal, and the same word inside L2-M1's malsseumhaseyo. A teacher's words are malsseum; using mal about them is the error, not merely the plainer choice.

sentences.trap: malsseum IS NOT A POLITER TONE, IT IS A DIFFERENT WORD. English has one noun for speech and adjusts the sentence around it. Korean swaps the noun itself, and the swap is obligatory once the speaker is somebody you raise.
sentences.sound: seon-SAENG-nim MAL-sseu-meun HANG-sang MA-ja-yo. malsseum-eun is said mal-sseu-meun.

variations.cue: What the teacher says is right.
variations.changed: -i rather than -eun, because the words are new to the account

variations.cue: My friend is always right.
variations.changed: the plain mal, on somebody you do not raise

mistake.why: A teacher's words are malsseum: Seonsaengnim malsseum-eun hangsang majayo.

sentences.usage: Agreeing with somebody senior when they are not in the room.

sentences.cue: The teacher said there's no exam tomorrow.

words.note: L1-M3's eopseoyo reported. It behaves like a describing verb, so the plain shape is the bare eopda with no n inserted: eopdago.

sentences.trap: EVERYTHING IN THIS SENTENCE IS THE MODULE AT ONCE. The teacher's tomorrow stays tomorrow, her present stays present, her jeo is gone, the ending is the describing-verb shape, and the only thing that moved is the register — which is on the chip and on the title, not on the verb.
sentences.sound: seon-SAENG-ni-mi NAE-il SI-heo-mi EOP-da-go HAE-sseo-yo. eopdago is said eop-tta-go.

variations.cue: My friend said there's no exam tomorrow.
variations.changed: a friend as the source — the same words, a neutral line

variations.cue: The teacher said there's no exam today.
variations.changed: the day inside the quote

mistake.why: The backshift again. She said there is none tomorrow, so the report keeps the present: Seonsaengnim-i naeil siheom-i eopdago haesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Passing on news from a class you were both in.

comprehensionPool.cue: My friend said he's coming tomorrow.
My friend said this restaurant is good.
My friend said she's learning Korean.
The teacher said to come tomorrow.
My friend said let's go together.
My friend asked whether I'm coming tomorrow.
What the teacher says is always right.
The teacher said there's no exam tomorrow.
My friend asked where I'm going.
